## Credit Allocation and Macroeconomic Fluctuations

Author: Daria Palitzsch

Welcome to my Problem Set, which is part of my master thesis at the University of Ulm. In the following analysis, we explore and discuss the relationship between credit allocation and macroeconomic fluctuations. The Problem Set is based on the empirical analysis presented in the paper [Credit Allocation and Macroeconomic Fluctuations](https://doi.org/10.1093/restud/rdad112) by Karsten Müller and Emil Verner (2024). The accompanying data and Stata replication code can be found [here](https://zenodo.org/records/8347045). The paper’s [Online Appendix](https://www.nber.org/appendix/w31420/manuscript_ReStud_CondAccept_appendix.pdf) provides additional results and robustness checks.

**Note:** Please open all external links in a new tab. This will prevent you from losing progress in the problem set.

The problem set is published here:

- **GitHub:**: https://github.com/DariaPalitzsch/RTutorCreditAllocation.git
- **ShinyApps:**: http://dariapalitzsch.shinyapps.io/RTutorCreditAllocationApp

Imagine credit expanding in two countries. In one, much of the additional lending reaches firms producing goods and services for international markets. In the other, it is concentrated among households and businesses serving domestic demand, such as construction companies and local service providers. How might these different borrowing patterns be related to GDP growth in the years afterwards?

Credit can support economic activity by expanding productive capacity or stimulating household demand (Mian, Sufi, & Verner, 2020, p. 949). At the same time, rapid credit growth helps predict financial crises (Schularick & Taylor, 2012, p. 1032). Yet not every credit boom ends in a crisis, suggesting that expansions can follow different economic paths (Gorton & Ordoñez, 2020, pp. 618–619). Understanding these differences requires us to examine what lies behind the aggregate increase in lending.

Müller and Verner investigate this question by distinguishing credit to households, tradable firms, and non-tradable firms. Tradable firms produce goods and services that can be sold across borders, whereas non-tradable firms primarily serve domestic markets. This distinction gives the problem set its central question: how is credit growth toward these different borrowers associated with real GDP growth during an expansion and in the years that follow?

To connect the economic question with the empirical analysis, we work through the data, variable construction, and estimation step by step. The problem set is therefore structured as follows:

In the first chapter, we become familiar with the structure of the dataset, the main credit variables, and the countries and years covered by the data. Building on this, the second chapter provides a descriptive introduction to credit allocation. We visualize the long-run development of private credit and examine how borrowing is distributed between households and firms and across different corporate sectors.

In the third chapter, we turn credit levels into measures of credit expansion. We calculate changes in credit-to-GDP ratios, compare different time windows, and examine how to limit the influence of extreme observations. The fourth chapter then turns to GDP growth. We distinguish growth during the credit expansion from growth in subsequent years and learn how to align the outcome windows with the timing of the credit variables.

In the fifth chapter, we begin the regression analysis and develop the specification step by step. Starting with a simple relationship between credit growth and GDP growth, we introduce the credit categories jointly, account for country differences, and examine the treatment of statistical uncertainty. We then compare the relationships observed during the expansion with those in its aftermath. The sixth chapter extends the analysis using local projections, allowing us to trace cumulative GDP paths over several horizons.

The seventh chapter examines how these local-projection paths change when we add year fixed effects or use credit changes dated in 2000 or earlier. We compare the estimates, their uncertainty, and sample coverage. The eighth chapter brings together the findings and their limitations. The optional appendix returns to three-year credit changes and examines financial fragility, other outcomes, further GDP-growth checks, and alternative industry classifications.

## Exercise 1 -- Data Overview

The Contents page introduced the relationship between credit allocation and economic performance. Before we study this relationship, we need to understand the data. We need to know which country and year each observation describes, what the credit variables measure, and which observations are available for comparison.

We first load and explore the dataset. We then look at the credit variables and follow one country over time. Finally, we check which countries, years, and credit values are available. This helps us choose the observations for each comparison and recognize where information is missing.

### 1.1 Loading and Summarizing the Dataset

Let us first look at the dataset we are working with. The file contains country identifiers, aggregate and sectoral credit measures, and macroeconomic variables over a long historical period.
Before we can inspect any of these observations, we must read in the data set. It is stored in RDS format and can be imported with the command `readRDS()`. 

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Just `check` the following code chunk to load the data set for this chapter.

```{r "2_1"}

```

The dataset is now stored in `data`.

To get a first impression of the dataset, let’s take a look at its first six observations. We can do that by calling the function `head()`. 

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Just `check` the following code chunk to display the first six observations of the dataset.

```{r "2_2"}
head(data)
```

As you can see, our dataset contains a large number of variables. We will need them all in the following analyses, but for now we focus on a selected subset. If you want to have a closer look at the data yourself, you can explore the loaded dataset in the **Data Explorer** tab. 

To get an overview of the dataset's size and coverage, we calculate a few summary statistics. We use the `dplyr` package for this. If you are not familiar with it, the info box below introduces its main commands.

info("dplyr")

The package is already installed for this problem set. The function `library()` makes its commands available in the current R session.

Let us first load it.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Enter the complete command that loads `dplyr`.

```{r "2_3"}
library(dplyr)
```

Let us now see how many observations, country units, and variables the dataset contains, and which years it covers. Inside `summarize()`, `n()` counts rows, `n_distinct()` counts unique values, and `ncol()` counts columns. The functions `min()` and `max()` identify the first and last recorded years.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Complete the three function names to count the country units and find the first and last years in the dataset.

```{r "2_4"}
dataset_overview <- data %>%
  summarize(
    Observations = n(),
    Country_units = n_distinct(country),
    First_year = min(year, na.rm = TRUE),
    Last_year = max(year, na.rm = TRUE),
    Variables = ncol(data)
  )

dataset_overview
```

The table gives an overview of the dataset’s size and time coverage. `Observations` reports the number of country-year observations, while `Country_units` counts the distinct country units represented in the data, including historical entities. `First_year` and `Last_year` indicate the earliest and latest years covered, and `Variables` gives the number of columns in the dataset.

### 1.2 Credit Variables and Their Roles

With 41 variables, reading the entire dataset at once would be overwhelming. A more useful starting point is one country-year observation. To understand it correctly, we need to answer three questions: **Which country and year does the row describe? Which type of credit is measured? And in what unit is it reported?**

The identifiers answer the first question. `countryname` contains the country name, and `year` identifies the point in time.

Both `country` and `id` identify the same country. The variable `country` contains a country code, while `id` provides an equivalent numerical identifier. In the following analysis, we use `country` to group observations and identify countries in the panel models.

The unit requires more thought. Imagine that two countries have the same nominal amount of outstanding credit but very different economic sizes. The same credit stock could be large relative to one economy and small relative to the other. To make the values more comparable, the main credit variables divide outstanding credit by nominal GDP. For country $i$ in year $t$, the ratio is

$$\text{Credit-to-GDP}_{i,t}=\frac{\text{outstanding credit}_{i,t}}{\text{nominal GDP}_{i,t}}\times 100.$$

The numerator is the outstanding stock of credit, while the denominator scales it by the size of the economy. Multiplication by 100 expresses the ratio as a percentage of GDP. Müller and Verner report total and sectoral private credit in this form; differences between two such ratios are measured in percentage points.

Suppose a credit variable equals `26.38`. The outstanding credit stock corresponds to 26.38 percent of annual GDP; this is **not** an annual growth rate. Changes in either credit or GDP can change the ratio.

info("Abbreviations used in the variable names")

We use four credit-to-GDP variables. `Total_GDP` measures total private credit to households and firms relative to GDP and is used for the descriptive analysis in Chapter 2. `HH_GDP` measures household (**HH**) credit, while `T_GDP` and `NT_GDP` measure credit to firms in tradable (**T**) and non-tradable (**NT**) sectors. In Chapter 3, we use these three credit-to-GDP levels to calculate the credit expansions included in the regressions.

The credit data measure outstanding claims of financial institutions on the domestic private sector. In most countries, these mainly consist of loans, so the measures do not capture every form of private debt.

The package `modelsummary` provides descriptive summaries and regression tables. We first use its `datasummary_skim()` function to summarize the credit variables. Before calling it, let us load the package.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Enter the complete command that loads `modelsummary`.

```{r "2_5"}
library(modelsummary)
```

Before following one country over time, let us see how these measures are distributed across the full dataset. `datasummary_skim()` provides the percentage of missing observations together with the mean, standard deviation, minimum, median, maximum, and a small histogram.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Add the four credit-to-GDP variables to `select()` in the order total, household, tradable-sector, and non-tradable-sector credit.

```{r "2_6"}
datasummary_skim(
  data %>%
    select(Total_GDP, HH_GDP, T_GDP, NT_GDP),
  output = "html"
)
```

The table shows that the credit variables cover very different ranges. `Total_GDP` ranges from about `0.2` to `959.8` percent of GDP. The maximum values of `HH_GDP`, `T_GDP`, and `NT_GDP` are approximately `125.0`, `47.4`, and `85.9`, respectively. In every case, the median lies far below the maximum. Most observations are therefore much less extreme than the largest recorded values.

Before we continue, keep in mind that `T_GDP` and `NT_GDP` include only selected categories of firm credit, not all firm lending. Adding these two variables and `HH_GDP` therefore does not give total private credit. For total private credit, we use the directly observed variable `Total_GDP`.

- The nominal household credit stock increased by 0.92 percent. [ ]

- The household credit-to-GDP ratio increased by 0.92 percent. [ ]

- The nominal household credit stock increased by 27.30 percent. [ ]

- The household credit-to-GDP ratio increased by 0.92 percentage points. [x]


### 1.3 Reading the Panel: Germany

Germany provides a concrete example of the panel structure. Instead of looking at one isolated observation, we select four consecutive years and ask what stays constant and what changes across the rows.

To make the table easier to read, we round the three credit variables to two decimal places.

info("Applying the same operation to several columns")

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Complete the filter to select Germany and the years from 1968 to 1971.

```{r "2_7"}
germany_example <- data %>%
  filter(
    countryname == "Germany",
    year >= 1968,
    year <= 1971
  ) %>%
  select(country, countryname, id, year, HH_GDP, T_GDP, NT_GDP) %>%
  mutate(across(c(HH_GDP, T_GDP, NT_GDP), ~ round(.x, 2)))

germany_example
```

Compare the identifiers and years across the displayed rows.


Quiz: Which feature of the Germany extract illustrates the time dimension of the full country panel?

- The observation year stays the same while the country identifier changes. [ ]

- The country identifier stays the same while the observation year changes. [x]

- The country identifier and observation year both change across the rows. [ ]

- The country identifier and observation year both remain unchanged across rows. [ ]


Germany gives us a complete sequence of annual observations in this example, but this is not the case for every country in the full dataset. Let us now check which countries, years, and credit values are available.

### 1.4 Geographic Coverage and Missing Data

Which regions does the dataset cover? The variable `wb_region` uses the World Bank regional classification recorded on 9 October 2026 to assign country units to regions. The following table compares the number of country units in our dataset with the total number of economies in each World Bank region.

The function `kable()` from `knitr` turns a data frame into a table. The package `kableExtra` provides functions such as `kable_classic()` and `kable_styling()` to format the table. We use both packages below, so we load them together.

If you are not familiar with `kableExtra` yet, you can find a brief introduction in the info box below.

info("kableExtra")

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Enter the two complete commands that load `knitr` and `kableExtra`.

```{r "2_8"}
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
```

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Just `check` the following code chunk to display the geographic coverage of the dataset.

```{r "2_9"}
country_coverage <- data %>%
  filter(!is.na(wb_region)) %>%
  distinct(country, wb_region, wb_region_economies) %>%
  group_by(wb_region, wb_region_economies) %>%
  summarize(Countries_in_data = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  select(wb_region, Countries_in_data, wb_region_economies)

kable(
  country_coverage,
  col.names = c(
    "World Bank region", "Countries in data",
    "Economies in region"
  ),
  row.names = FALSE
) %>%
  kable_classic() %>%
  kable_styling(font_size = 15, full_width = F)
```

The regional totals follow the [World Bank Country and Lending Groups](https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/906519-world-bank-country-and-lending-groups), accessed on 9 October 2026 (World Bank, n.d.-a). This regional classification is separate from the fixed 2019 income classification used for the advanced/emerging distinction later in the problem set (Müller & Verner, 2024, p. 3653, Figure 1). The table includes country units from all major regions. However, a country can appear in the table even if some years or variables are missing. One historical country unit is excluded because it has no region in the current World Bank classification.

Let us now look at the years covered by the dataset. The first and last recorded years can differ between countries, and some years in between may be missing. We count the recorded years for each country and compare this number with the total number of years from its first to its last observation. If fewer years are recorded, at least one year in between is missing.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Just `check` the following code chunk to summarize how many years are recorded for each country and check for gaps.

```{r "2_10"}
country_histories <- data %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarize(
    Recorded_years = n_distinct(year),
    Internal_gap = max(year) - min(year) + 1 > n_distinct(year),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

history_overview <- country_histories %>%
  summarize(
    Country_units = n(),
    Shortest_history = min(Recorded_years),
    Median_history = median(Recorded_years),
    Longest_history = max(Recorded_years),
    Histories_with_gaps = sum(Internal_gap)
  )

history_overview
```

The output shows `217` country units with `6` to `105` recorded years and a median of `65` recorded years. For `17` country units, at least one year between the first and last observations is missing. The dataset is therefore an **unbalanced panel**: not every country contributes the same years.

Even if a country and year appear in the dataset, a credit value for that observation may still be missing. Section 1.2 reported missing values as a percentage. We now count the exact numbers of available and missing values. `is.na(x)` identifies missing entries, while `!is.na(x)` identifies values that are available.

We use `sapply()` to repeat the same calculation for each column of `credit_levels`. In `function(x)`, `x` stands for one column at a time. `sum(is.na(x))` counts the missing values in that column, while `sum(!is.na(x))` counts the available values.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Complete the function that identifies missing values to create a table of available and missing values for each credit variable.

```{r "2_11"}
credit_levels <- data[, c(
  "Total_GDP", "HH_GDP", "T_GDP", "NT_GDP"
)]

credit_availability <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(credit_levels),
  Available = sapply(credit_levels, function(x) sum(!is.na(x))),
  Missing = sapply(credit_levels, function(x) sum(is.na(x)))
)

kable(credit_availability, row.names = FALSE) %>%
  kable_classic() %>%
  kable_styling(font_size = 15, full_width = F)
```

The table shows how often each credit variable is available. Although the dataset contains `14,916` country-year observations, `Total_GDP` is available for `9,740` of them. The corresponding counts are `4,481` for `HH_GDP`, `3,848` for `T_GDP`, and `2,998` for `NT_GDP`. A row can therefore contain the country and year even when one or more credit values are missing.

If we compare averages based on different country-year observations, some of the difference may come from which countries and years are included, rather than from the credit measures themselves.


Quiz: The dataset contains 14,916 country-year rows, but HH_GDP is observed for only 4,481; which interpretation is supported?

- All credit variables are unavailable whenever household-credit values are missing from a row. [ ]

- Household-credit values equal zero in every row where HH_GDP is recorded as missing. [ ]

- Household-credit values are unavailable for some country-year rows recorded in the dataset. [x]

- The available household-credit values cover every recorded year of each country in the dataset. [ ]


### Summary

The credit variables measure outstanding credit stocks relative to GDP. Their values should not be interpreted as annual growth rates. `T_GDP` and `NT_GDP` include only selected categories of firm credit. Adding them to household credit therefore does not give total private credit.

We also saw that countries have observations for different years and that some credit values are missing even when the country and year are recorded. Comparisons between credit variables may therefore use different country-year observations. When choosing samples throughout the problem set, we will check both which country-year observations are recorded and which credit values are available. In Chapter 2, we use the credit-to-GDP levels to explore economic patterns across countries and over time.

## Exercise 2 -- Descriptive Patterns in Credit Allocation

Now that we know what the variables measure and where data are available, let us examine how private credit is allocated. How has private credit changed relative to GDP? How is it divided between households and firms, and between different types of firms?

We first plot credit over time for four countries. We then compare household and firm credit in a larger sample before looking more closely at tradable and non-tradable firms. For each comparison, we explain which countries are included and how they are weighted. Finally, we discuss what the figures tell us about credit and GDP growth and what we still need to measure for the regression analysis.

This chapter presents adapted descriptive analyses of the authors’ data rather than exact reproductions of the paper’s figures.

Before we begin, we load `Data.rds` again.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Just `check` the following code chunk to load the data for this chapter.

```{r "3_1"}
data <- readRDS("Data.rds")
```

### Structure

2.1 Long-Run Rise in Private Credit

2.2 How Is Private Credit Distributed Between Households and Firms?

2.3 Where Is Classified Corporate Credit Concentrated?

2.4 What Descriptive Evidence Cannot Tell Us

2.5 From the Descriptive Data to the Main Analysis Sample

### 2.1 Long-Run Rise in Private Credit

Let us first examine how outstanding private credit has developed relative to GDP. We use `Total_GDP` to follow the United States, Germany, China, and Brazil from 1970 to 2014. These country histories introduce the paper’s evidence on the long-run rise in private credit.

Before drawing the figure, we select the four countries and the years from 1970 to 2014. All four countries have continuous observations for this period. We also assign each country to an economy group. The variable `advanced_economy` follows the World Bank's 2019 income classification: high-income countries form the advanced group, and all other countries form the emerging group. We use this fixed classification for all years so that we compare credit developments within consistently defined country groups.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Just `check` the following code to prepare the data.

```{r "3_2"}
credit_paths <- data %>%
  filter(
    country %in% c("USA", "DEU", "CHN", "BRA"),
    between(year, 1970, 2014)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    economy_group = factor(
      if_else(
        advanced_economy == 1,
        "Advanced economies",
        "Emerging economies"
      ),
      levels = c("Advanced economies", "Emerging economies")
    )
  )
```

We can now plot the credit-to-GDP ratios for these countries. We use `ggplot2` to put year on the horizontal axis and the credit ratio on the vertical axis, with a separate line for each country.

info("ggplot2")

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Enter the complete command that loads `ggplot2`.

```{r "3_3"}
library(ggplot2)
```

We can now draw the figure using `credit_paths`. The remaining code adds the lines, separates the economy groups, and formats the figure. 

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Complete `aes()` to place `year` on the horizontal axis and `Total_GDP` on the vertical axis. Use `countryname` to give each country line its own color.

```{r "3_4"}
ggplot(credit_paths, aes(x = year, y = Total_GDP, color = countryname)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~economy_group, nrow = 1) +
  scale_color_brewer(
    palette = "Dark2",
    breaks = c("Germany", "United States", "Brazil", "China")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Total private credit (% of GDP)",
    color = "",
    title = "Private credit across four economies",
    subtitle = "Two advanced and two emerging economies, 1970-2014"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Each line follows one country over time. The two panels separate advanced and emerging economies while using the same vertical scale. Compare how the credit ratios develop and where their paths change direction. These four countries are illustrative examples; their lines do not represent country-group averages.


Quiz: Which statement most accurately describes the four country paths?

- The countries within each panel share turning points, with differences mainly in the levels of their credit ratios. [ ]

- Germany and Brazil peak earlier, while both the US and China increase continuously without any intermediate declines. [ ]

- The two emerging-country examples rise more strongly, establishing a larger average increase for emerging economies as a group. [ ]

- All four ratios finish above their starting levels, but the timing and size of their increases differ. [x]


We now move beyond the four country examples and compare household and firm credit in a larger sample. We use population-weighted means for this comparison.

### 2.2 How Is Private Credit Distributed Between Households and Firms?

We divide total private credit into credit to households and credit to firms. The two credit series can develop differently. This distinction matters for economic performance: Mian, Sufi, and Verner (2017, p. 1755) find that increases in household debt relative to GDP predict lower GDP growth in later years.

`HH_GDP` measures household credit relative to GDP. For each country and year, we calculate overall firm credit relative to GDP as `Total_GDP - HH_GDP`.

info("How sectoral firm credit is constructed")

We use 1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, and 2010, as well as 2014, the final year in the sample. We choose years at regular ten-year intervals to avoid selecting only years that fit a simple trend. We store these six benchmark years in `benchmark_years`.

We include every country with both `Total_GDP` and `HH_GDP` available in all six benchmark years. We also need its population in 2000 for the weights. Let us first check how many countries meet these requirements.

We use `complete.cases()` to check whether several variables are available in each row. Here, `complete.cases(Total_GDP, HH_GDP)` returns `TRUE` when both credit values are observed. Since the data are grouped by country, `all()` checks whether this holds for every selected benchmark year. The filter therefore keeps only countries with both credit measures available in all six years.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Just `check` the following code chunk to define the benchmark years and select the countries for this comparison. The output shows how many countries are included.

```{r "3_5"}
benchmark_years <- c(1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010, 2014)

borrower_sample <- data %>%
  filter(year %in% benchmark_years, !is.na(pop2000)) %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  filter(
    n_distinct(year) == length(benchmark_years),
    all(complete.cases(Total_GDP, HH_GDP))
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

borrower_sample %>%
  summarize(Countries = n_distinct(country))
```

The output shows that `40` countries meet these requirements. We use the same countries in every benchmark year, so changes between the bars cannot be caused by countries entering or leaving the sample. We weight each country's credit-to-GDP ratio by its population in 2000:

$$\bar{x}_{t}^{w}=\frac{\sum_i \mathrm{pop2000}_{i}x_{i,t}}{\sum_i \mathrm{pop2000}_{i}}.$$

We use population weights because we want credit developments in countries where more people live to have greater influence on the comparison. All bars use the same countries and population weights. We calculate a population-weighted mean of the countries' credit-to-GDP ratios. This differs from adding up credit and GDP across countries and then dividing the two totals. The dataset provides population in 2000 (`pop2000`), rather than annual population, so the weights reflect country size at that fixed date.


Quiz: Country A has twice country B's population in 2000; how are their ratios weighted in every benchmark year?

- Country A's ratio receives twice country B's weight in every benchmark year. [x]

- Both countries' ratios receive equal weights because each is already scaled by GDP. [ ]

- Country A's ratio receives twice country B's weight only in the year 2000. [ ]

- Both countries' ratios receive weights proportional to their GDP in every benchmark year. [ ]


The function `pivot_longer()` from `tidyr` rearranges the two weighted credit measures for the plot without changing their values. Let us load the package before using the function.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Enter the complete command that loads `tidyr`.

```{r "3_6"}
library(tidyr)
```

In `pivot_longer()`, `cols` selects the columns to combine. `names_to = "Borrower"` stores their column names in a new column, while `values_to = "Credit"` stores the corresponding numerical values.

**Note:** The column names contain spaces. Enter them in backticks, for example `` `Firm credit` ``. Backticks are different from ordinary single quotation marks.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Select firm credit followed by household credit in `cols` to reshape the two columns with `pivot_longer()`.

```{r "3_7"}
credit_composition <- borrower_sample %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarize(
    `Household credit` = weighted.mean(HH_GDP, w = pop2000),
    `Firm credit` = weighted.mean(Total_GDP - HH_GDP, w = pop2000),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(`Firm credit`, `Household credit`),
    names_to = "Borrower",
    values_to = "Credit"
  ) 
```

The prepared dataset `credit_composition` now contains the population-weighted means for household and firm credit in each benchmark year. We will use a stacked bar chart to compare these two components over time. Each bar represents one benchmark year, with separate colored segments for household and firm credit. In the following code, `geom_col()` draws the bars from the calculated values, while `fill = Borrower` distinguishes the two components by color.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Just `check` the following code chunk to display the borrower-composition plot using the prepared dataset `credit_composition`.

```{r "3_8"}
ggplot(credit_composition, aes(x = factor(year), y = Credit, fill = Borrower)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Paired") +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Population-weighted mean (% of GDP)",
    fill = "",
    title = "How is private credit divided between borrowers?",
    subtitle = "Population-weighted means for a fixed 40-country sample"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The horizontal axis shows the benchmark years, and the vertical axis shows population-weighted means of country credit-to-GDP ratios. Each bar contains one segment for household credit and one for firm credit. Both use the same observations and weights, so the total bar height equals the population-weighted mean of `Total_GDP` in that year. Compare the size of the two colored segments as well as the total bar height.


Quiz: Comparing the first and final bars, which statement is supported for the fixed 40-country sample?

- Both components rise, firm credit increases more, and firm credit remains the larger component in the final year. [ ]

- Both components rise, household credit increases more, and household credit becomes the larger component in the final year. [ ]

- Both components rise, household credit increases more, and firm credit remains slightly larger in the final year. [x]

- Household credit rises while firm credit falls, and household credit becomes the larger component in the final year. [ ]


Household credit can increase more than firm credit and still remain smaller at the end of the period. This comparison describes the weighted sample; it does not mean that every country followed the same pattern.

### 2.3 Where Is Classified Corporate Credit Concentrated?

In the previous section, we compared household and firm credit. We now take a closer look at firm credit. Using the available sectoral data, we compare credit to firms in tradable sectors (`T_GDP`) with credit to firms in non-tradable sectors (`NT_GDP`).

Credit supply expansions can affect economic activity through productive capacity or household demand (Mian, Sufi, & Verner, 2020, p. 949). Our sectoral distinction asks a related question: whether credit expands toward tradable firms or toward non-tradable activities such as construction, real estate, and local services (Müller & Verner, 2024, p. 3645). Which of the two components is larger in our sample: credit to firms in tradable sectors or credit to firms in non-tradable sectors?

Fewer countries have data on tradable and non-tradable credit than on household credit. As before, we include only countries with both credit measures available in all six benchmark years and a recorded population in 2000.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Just `check` the following code chunk to select the countries for the sectoral comparison and display how many are included.

```{r "3_9"}
sector_sample <- data %>%
  filter(year %in% benchmark_years, !is.na(pop2000)) %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  filter(
    n_distinct(year) == length(benchmark_years),
    all(complete.cases(T_GDP, NT_GDP))
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

sector_sample %>%
  summarize(Countries = n_distinct(country))
```

The output shows that `20` countries meet these requirements, compared with `40` in the comparison of household and firm credit. Fewer countries have both sectoral variables available in every benchmark year. We again use population in 2000 (`pop2000`) for the weights. Because the two plots use different country samples, we compare changes over time within each plot rather than comparing their absolute levels.

We use a dumbbell plot to compare the two population-weighted means in each benchmark year. It shows the two values as points connected by a line.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Enter the two sectoral variables to calculate their population-weighted means for the selected countries.

```{r "3_10"}
sector_credit_benchmarks <- sector_sample %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarize(
    tradable = weighted.mean(T_GDP, w = pop2000),
    non_tradable = weighted.mean(NT_GDP, w = pop2000),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(gap = non_tradable - tradable)
```

For each benchmark year, `geom_segment()` draws a horizontal line between the two weighted means. `x = tradable` sets the starting point, while `xend` sets the endpoint. The benchmark year is defined by `y` in `ggplot()`. With `yend = factor(year)`, the endpoint uses the same year, so the line stays horizontal.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Complete `xend` so that each line connects the tradable and non-tradable credit means.

```{r "3_11"}
ggplot(sector_credit_benchmarks, aes(y = factor(year))) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = tradable, xend = non_tradable, yend = factor(year)),
    color = "grey65",
    linewidth = 1.4
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(x = tradable, color = "Tradable sectors"), size = 3.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = non_tradable, color = "Non-tradable sectors"), size = 3.5) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Paired") +
  labs(
    x = "Population-weighted mean (% of GDP)",
    y = "Year",
    color = "",
    title = "Where is Classified Corporate Credit Concentrated?",
    subtitle = "Fixed 20-country sample; distance between points is the sectoral gap"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The horizontal axis shows population-weighted means of outstanding credit as a percentage of GDP, and the vertical axis lists the benchmark years. Each row has two points, one for each sectoral credit measure. The colors identify the sectors, and a grey line connects the points. The point farther to the right has the larger weighted mean. A longer line indicates a larger gap between the two means. Use the plot to compare the components over time.


Quiz: Which statement best describes the population-weighted credit-to-GDP means in the dumbbell plot?

- Tradable credit starts slightly larger and remains larger, with the gap widening after a temporary narrowing around 1980. [ ]

- Tradable credit starts slightly larger, the means nearly coincide in 1980, and non-tradable credit subsequently pulls ahead. [x]

- Non-tradable credit starts larger and remains larger, with the gap narrowing substantially after its peak around 2010. [ ]

- Tradable credit starts slightly larger, non-tradable credit overtakes it, and their gap becomes smaller after 1990. [ ]


The plot shows how firm credit differs between the two classified sectors. It does not show that existing loans moved from one sector to the other. The points represent outstanding credit relative to GDP, not new loans issued during a period.

### 2.4 What Descriptive Evidence Cannot Tell Us

What do these figures tell us about GDP growth? They show credit-to-GDP levels, but do not link changes in these ratios during a particular period to GDP growth afterwards. A high credit ratio may reflect borrowing from recent years or much earlier. The weighted means also hide differences between individual countries.

We therefore ask:

**How is an increase in a country's credit-to-GDP ratio over a given period related to later GDP growth? Does this relationship differ between credit to households, tradable firms, and non-tradable firms?**

To answer this question, we need to examine each country and year instead of averaging across countries. Before we calculate changes in credit-to-GDP ratios and GDP-growth measures, we first identify the observations that meet the sample requirements for the main analysis.


Quiz: Which measures match our question about changes in credit-to-GDP ratios and subsequent economic growth?

- Country-level changes in credit-to-GDP ratios over a defined period and GDP growth afterwards. [x]

- Country-level credit-to-GDP levels at one date and GDP growth over the following years. [ ]

- Population-weighted changes in group-average credit ratios and GDP levels in the final benchmark year. [ ]

- Country-level changes in nominal credit stocks and GDP levels at the beginning of the period. [ ]


### 2.5 From the Descriptive Data to the Main Analysis Sample

We now return to the full dataset to prepare the sample for the GDP regressions. We apply the sample criteria used by the authors to determine which countries and observations can be included in the analysis.

Müller and Verner restrict their main analysis to countries with more than one million inhabitants in 2000 so that unusually large fluctuations in very small economies do not dominate the results. A country must also have at least ten years with data on both tradable and non-tradable credit. These years do not have to be consecutive. Within such a country, an observation meets the criteria only if both sectoral credit measures are available in that year. The variable `pop2000` records population in 2000. We use `sectoral_years` to count the years with both credit measures available for each country.

We create the binary indicator `smp_GDP` to mark the observations that meet these rules. It takes the value `1` when the population and sectoral-data requirements are satisfied. This indicator does not identify credit booms. Further checks are needed to determine whether all variables required for a regression are available.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Complete the population threshold and the minimum number of years with both sectoral credit measures available to construct `smp_GDP`.

```{r "3_12"}
data <- data %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  mutate(
    sectoral_years = sum(!is.na(T_GDP) & !is.na(NT_GDP)),
    smp_GDP = as.integer(
      pop2000 > 1000000 &
      sectoral_years >= 10 &
      !is.na(T_GDP) &
      !is.na(NT_GDP)
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```

Creating `smp_GDP` marks the observations that meet these requirements; it does not remove any rows from `data`. Let us now use it to count the observations and countries that meet the requirements and find out which years they cover.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Complete the command that counts the countries. The supplied filter keeps observations with `smp_GDP == 1`.

```{r "3_13"}
sample_overview <- data %>%
  filter(smp_GDP == 1) %>%
  summarize(
    Observations = n(),
    Countries = n_distinct(country),
    First_year = min(year),
    Last_year = max(year)
  )

sample_overview
```

The table shows `2,324` country-year observations from `76` countries between 1946 and 2014 that meet these requirements. For the later analysis, we also need GDP growth and the credit-change measures used in each comparison. We check which observations have these values available in the following chapters.


Quiz: What does smp_GDP = 1 indicate for an observation's eligibility in later regressions?

- The observation meets sample criteria, so every regression already has all required variables. [ ]

- The country meets sample criteria, so all its years qualify despite missing sectoral data. [ ]

- The observation meets sample criteria, but required regression variables must also be observed. [x]

- The observation meets sample criteria and records rising credit in at least one category. [ ]


### Summary

All four country examples have higher credit ratios at the end than at the beginning, but the paths between these years differ. In the comparison of household and firm credit, household credit increases more between the first and final benchmark years, although firm credit remains slightly larger at the end. In the sectoral comparison, tradable credit has the larger weighted mean at first. Non-tradable credit becomes larger later, and the gap grows.

These findings describe the selected country samples. Using the same countries and weights in every benchmark year makes changes over time easier to compare. However, the plot of household and firm credit and the sectoral plot use different samples. Neither plot links changes in credit-to-GDP ratios during a particular period to later economic performance. We have also marked the observations that meet the population and sectoral-data requirements for the GDP analysis. For each regression, we still need to check that the GDP-growth outcome and all explanatory variables are available. In the next chapter, we calculate changes in credit-to-GDP ratios to distinguish recent expansions from existing credit levels.


## Exercise 3 -- Measuring Credit Expansions

Chapter 2 described outstanding credit relative to GDP and how it is divided between borrowers. We now turn to changes in credit-to-GDP ratios to study how credit expansions are related to economic performance. A high ratio may reflect borrowing accumulated long ago, while a country with a lower ratio may have experienced a large recent increase.

We start by measuring credit expansions using credit to firms in non-tradable sectors. We explain which time window we use, which observations we need, and how these choices affect the interpretation. Let us begin by loading the dataset.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Just `check` the following code chunk to load the dataset for this chapter.

```{r "4_1"}
data <- readRDS("Data.rds")
```

### Structure

3.1 From Credit Levels to Three-Year Credit Changes

3.2 Comparing One- and Three-Year Credit Changes

3.3 Comparing Credit Changes Across Borrower Groups

3.4 Preventing Extreme Episodes from Dominating

### 3.1 From Credit Levels to Three-Year Credit Changes

Suppose two countries both have a non-tradable credit-to-GDP ratio of 20 percent today. In the first country, the ratio was already 20 percent at the beginning of the period. In the second, it rose from 10 to 20 percent. Their current credit ratios are identical, but their recent credit developments differ substantially.

To distinguish these developments, we need to examine changes in credit-to-GDP ratios rather than their current levels. We therefore compare the ratio at the end of a period with its value at the beginning.

But how far back should we look? Which time window is suitable for capturing the credit buildup we want to study?

A one-year window focuses on annual movements. A longer window captures changes accumulated over several years, but may also combine different stages of a credit cycle. The choice therefore depends on the economic development we want to study. It also affects data availability, because calculating the change requires an observed value at the earlier endpoint.

The authors choose a three-year window to measure credit expansions. Their evidence on credit booms shows a rapid buildup over approximately three to four years. This motivates a measure that captures developments over several years rather than annual movements alone. We adopt this three-year window for the replication.

With the window fixed, we can construct the measure. For non-tradable credit, the three-year change is the current credit-to-GDP ratio minus its value three calendar years earlier:

$$D3NT\_GDP_{i,t}=NT\_GDP_{i,t}-NT\_GDP_{i,t-3}.$$

Because both terms are credit-to-GDP ratios, their difference is measured in **percentage points of GDP**. For example, if `NT_GDP` rises from 10 to 12 percent of GDP, the increase is 2 percentage points. This describes the difference between the two ratios, not a percentage growth rate.

To calculate the three-year change, we need the credit value from exactly three years earlier. Some country histories contain gaps, so moving back three rows with `lag(x, 3)` could select a different year. We therefore use `match(year - 3, year)` within each country to find the correct row. We then take the corresponding value of `NT_GDP`.

Only the values at the beginning and end of the three-year window are needed. If either year or its credit value is missing, the change is set to `NA`. If years between the two dates are missing, our calculation is not affected.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Enter the number of calendar years to look backward and construct `D3NT_GDP`.

```{r "4_2"}
data <- data %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    D3NT_GDP = NT_GDP - NT_GDP[match(year - 3, year)]
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```


Quiz: Suppose NT_GDP rises from 15 to 20 between t - 3 and t; what does D3NT_GDP = 5 tell us?

- The ratio rose by 5 percentage points in each of the three intervening years. [ ]

- The ratio is 5 percentage points higher, without implying increases in every intervening year. [x]

- The nominal credit stock rose by 5 percent over the full three-year period. [ ]

- New lending accumulated to 5 percent of GDP over the full three-year period. [ ]



Quiz: A country has observations in 2015, 2016, 2018, and 2019; which observed credit value is needed for its three-year change in 2019?

- Use the 2015 value, which lies three observed rows before the current 2019 observation. [ ]

- Use the 2018 value, which is the most recent observed value before the 2019 observation. [ ]

- Use no earlier value, because the missing 2017 observation makes the three-year change unavailable. [ ]

- Use the 2016 value, which lies exactly three calendar years before the 2019 observation. [x]


info("Related evidence on household debt")

### 3.2 Comparing One- and Three-Year Credit Changes

We have now constructed the three-year credit change used in the replication. Let us compare it with the supplied annual change.

`D1NT_GDP` and `D3NT_GDP` describe changes in the same credit-to-GDP ratio over different periods. Both are measured in percentage points, but the three-year measure covers a longer buildup. We compare their distributions and check how many observations are available for each measure.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Add the three-year variable you just constructed to the `select()` command.

```{r "4_3"}
datasummary_skim(
  data %>%
    filter(smp_GDP == 1) %>%
    select(D1NT_GDP, D3NT_GDP),
  output = "html"
)
```


Quiz: What does this table show when we move from the one-year to the three-year credit-change measure?

- The higher three-year mean shows faster annual growth of the credit ratio across all countries. [ ]

- The three-year measure covers a longer period and is available for fewer observations here. [x]

- The one-year measure captures the same multi-year expansion while requiring fewer observed credit values. [ ]

- The lower one-year standard deviation proves that this window measures credit expansions more accurately. [ ]


For the one-year change, the mean and median are both about `0.2` percentage points. For the three-year change, the mean is about `0.8` and the median is `0.5` percentage points. The three-year changes also have a wider range, from about `-32.2` to `35.5`. These values cover three years, so the higher mean does not show that credit grew faster each year.

Missing values are also more common for the three-year change: `11` percent, compared with `4` percent for the one-year change. Looking further back leaves fewer observations with both credit values needed for the calculation. The two summaries therefore use different sets of country-year observations.

The table shows how a longer window changes both the measured credit expansion and the number of observations we can use. It does not tell us which window is best for the research question.

### 3.3 Comparing Credit Changes Across Borrower Groups

Suppose `D3NT_GDP` equals `5`. Does this mean that the credit expansion was concentrated in non-tradable sectors? Not necessarily. Credit-to-GDP ratios for tradable firms and households may have stayed constant or increased at the same time. The same rise in the non-tradable ratio can therefore be part of either a concentrated sectoral expansion or a broader credit expansion. This comparison concerns the three observed credit categories, which do not cover every component of private credit.

We therefore compare changes in the three credit-to-GDP ratios over the same window. Alongside `D3NT_GDP`, the prepared variables `D3T_GDP` and `D3HH_GDP` measure the corresponding changes for firms in tradable sectors and for households. For each `D3` variable, a value of `1` means that the corresponding credit-to-GDP ratio rose by one percentage point from `t - 3` to `t`.

If the tradable and household credit changes stay the same, a larger non-tradable change also means a larger combined expansion across the three categories. This is different from shifting a fixed amount of credit from one borrower group to another.


Quiz: Country A has three-year credit-to-GDP changes of 0 for tradable sectors, 5 for non-tradable sectors, and 0 for households, while B records 4, 5, and 3; which comparison is supported across these categories?

- A's expansion is concentrated in non-tradable credit, whereas B's extends across all three categories. [x]

- B's expansion is more concentrated because its combined increase across the three categories is larger. [ ]

- Both expansions are equally concentrated because their non-tradable credit changes have the same size. [ ]

- Neither expansion can be compared because the three categories exclude some components of total credit. [ ]


### 3.4 Preventing Extreme Episodes from Dominating

We now have credit-change measures for all three borrower groups. Before we study how these credit changes are related to GDP growth, there is one more issue to consider: a few unusually large increases or decreases can have a strong influence on our results. We therefore set a lower and an upper limit and replace values outside these limits with the nearest cutoff. All observations remain in the dataset. This procedure is called winsorization (Dixon & Tukey, 1968, p. 83).

Following the authors, we use the first and ninety-ninth percentiles as our cutoffs. Values below the first percentile are replaced by the first-percentile value. Values above the ninety-ninth percentile are replaced by the ninety-ninth-percentile value. Values between these limits stay unchanged. Unlike trimming, winsorization adjusts extreme values rather than removing observations.

We calculate the cutoffs separately for each credit-change variable, using its available values in the full dataset before we apply the `smp_GDP` restriction. 

info("Replicating the authors' winsorization in R")

Let us first define the function. Once defined, it remains available throughout the problem set. We will then apply it to the non-tradable credit-change variable and compare the original and winsorized values.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Just `check` the following code chunk to define `winsorize()`.

```{r "4_4"}
winsorize <- function(x) {
  limits <- stats::quantile(
    x,
    probs = c(0.01, 0.99),
    na.rm = TRUE,
    type = 1
  )
  pmin(pmax(x, limits[1]), limits[2])
}
```

Let us first use a simple example to check which values the function changes.


Quiz: Suppose the first- and ninety-ninth-percentile cutoffs are -10 and 15; what does winsorization do to c(-20, 4, NA, 30)?

- It returns c(NA, 4, NA, NA). [ ]

- It returns c(-10, 4, 0, 15). [ ]

- It returns c(-20, 4, NA, 30). [ ]

- It returns c(-10, 4, NA, 15). [x]


We now apply `winsorize()` to `D3NT_GDP`. We calculate the cutoffs using the full dataset before keeping the observations with `smp_GDP = 1`. This keeps the cutoffs the same across later comparisons.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Apply our `winsorize()` function to `D3NT_GDP`. The supplied code then keeps the observations selected by `smp_GDP` and compares the raw and winsorized values.

```{r "4_5"}
data <- data %>%
  mutate(D3NT_GDP_w = winsorize(D3NT_GDP)) %>%
  filter(smp_GDP == 1)

datasummary_skim(
  data %>%
    transmute(Raw = D3NT_GDP, Winsorized = D3NT_GDP_w),
  fmt = 2,
  output = "html"
)
```

The table shows that the mean changes only slightly, from about `0.76` to `0.77`, while the median stays at `0.53`. The largest changes occur at the extremes: the minimum rises from about `-32.19` to `-11.91`, and the maximum falls from `35.49` to `15.33`. The share of missing values stays at `11` percent.

These statistics describe the observations with `smp_GDP = 1`. The cutoffs, however, were calculated using the full dataset before this selection.

Winsorization limits the size of extreme values, but it does not tell us whether they reflect measurement errors or genuine economic episodes. The authors report that their main results are similar without winsorization.

### Summary

We now measure changes in credit-to-GDP ratios over three calendar years, using exact endpoints rather than counting a fixed number of rows. Winsorization caps extreme values without removing observations and leaves the percentage-point units unchanged. Comparing the changes for all three borrower categories helps us distinguish an expansion concentrated in non-tradable sectors from a broader increase across categories.

  <thead>
    <tr><th>Credit level</th><th>Three-year change</th><th>Winsorized change</th></tr>

    <tr><td><code>NT_GDP</code></td><td><code>D3NT_GDP</code></td><td><code>D3NT_GDP_w</code></td></tr>

</table>

The table links each credit-to-GDP ratio to its three-year change and winsorized version. We constructed these measures for non-tradable credit; the household and tradable variables follow the same rules. We use `Total_GDP` to describe overall credit levels, while the later analysis focuses on changes for the three borrower groups.

We calculated the changes and cutoffs using the full country histories before selecting observations with `smp_GDP = 1`. This keeps earlier credit values available and gives us the same cutoffs for later comparisons. Chapter 4 now introduces GDP-growth measures to study economic performance during and after these credit expansions.

## Exercise 4 -- Timing GDP Growth Around Credit Expansions

In Chapter 3, we measured changes in credit-to-GDP ratios over three-year periods. We now construct GDP-growth measures to examine economic activity during and after those periods. GDP growth over the same years as the credit expansion tells us what happened during the expansion, while growth over later years tells us what happened afterwards.

We first define how real GDP growth is measured and which dates each outcome covers. We then move the GDP-growth window forward while keeping the credit window fixed. We calculate these outcomes using the full country histories and apply the `smp_GDP` restriction only after retrieving the required GDP endpoints.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Just `check` the following code chunk to load the dataset for this chapter.

```{r "5_1"}
data <- readRDS("Data.rds")
```

### Structure

4.1 Measuring Economic Performance

4.2 Separating the Expansion Phase from the Aftermath

4.3 Calculating GDP Growth for Different Time Windows

### 4.1 Measuring Economic Performance

Suppose two countries experience the same credit expansion, but one economy is much larger than the other. Comparing their GDP levels would mainly tell us which country is larger. We want to examine how economic activity changed within each country, so we use GDP growth.

We use **real GDP**, which removes the effect of changes in domestic prices (World Bank, n.d.-b). Our measure refers to total GDP, not GDP per capita. The variable `log_real_gdp` stores 100 times the natural logarithm of real GDP. Differences in this variable measure growth in **log points**, giving us a common unit for comparing growth across countries.

To match the three-year credit window, we subtract the value of `log_real_gdp` three years earlier from its current value:

$$\mathrm{gdp\_3yr\_h0}_{i,t}=\mathrm{log\_real\_gdp}_{i,t}-\mathrm{log\_real\_gdp}_{i,t-3}.$$

The factor of 100 is already included in `log_real_gdp`, so we do not multiply the difference by 100 again in R. A value of `10` means that real GDP grew by ten log points over the three years. For moderate changes, log points are close to percentage changes. More precisely, ten log points correspond to $100(e^{0.10}-1)\approx10.5$ percent growth over the full period.

The suffix `h0` means that the GDP-growth window has not been shifted forward: the credit-to-GDP change and GDP growth both cover `t - 3` to `t`. To construct the outcome, `calendar_lead()` retrieves a value for the exact year `t + h`, and `calendar_growth()` uses the two GDP endpoints to calculate growth. We start with `h = 0`. Both helper functions remain available in later chapters.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Enter the horizon that aligns the GDP-growth window with the credit expansion and create `gdp_3yr_h0`.

```{r "5_2"}
calendar_lead <- function(x, year, h) {
  target_row <- match(year + h, year)
  x[target_row]
}

calendar_growth <- function(x, year, h, window = 3) {
  end_value <- calendar_lead(x, year, h)
  start_value <- calendar_lead(x, year, h - window)
  end_value - start_value
}

data <- data %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    gdp_3yr_h0 = calendar_growth(log_real_gdp, year, 0)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```

For Germany in 2000, let us convert the log-point value into its exact percentage equivalent.

<b style="color:green">Task:</b> Complete the conversion from log points to percent.

```{r "5_3"}
data %>%
  filter(countryname == "Germany", year == 2000) %>%
  mutate(
    year,
    `GDP growth (log points)` = round(gdp_3yr_h0, 2),
    `GDP growth (percent)` = round(
      100 * (exp(gdp_3yr_h0 / 100) - 1),
      2
    )
  ) %>%
  select(year, `GDP growth (log points)`, `GDP growth (percent)`)
```

Let us use the two values in the output to interpret Germany's real GDP growth over this period.


Quiz: Germany's gdp_3yr_h0 equals 6.95 log points, or approximately 7.20 percent, in 2000. Which interpretation is correct?

- Real GDP grew cumulatively by approximately 7.20 percent over the three years from 1997 to 2000. [x]

- Real GDP grew annually by approximately 7.20 percent in each year from 1997 to 2000. [ ]

- Real GDP in 2000 equaled approximately 7.20 percent of its level in the year 1997. [ ]

- Real GDP grew cumulatively by approximately 7.20 percent over the three years from 2000 to 2003. [ ]


### 4.2 Separating the Expansion Phase from the Aftermath

Imagine that a credit expansion runs from 1997 to 2000. GDP growth over those same years tells us what happened while credit was expanding, but not what happened from 2000 onwards. We therefore move the GDP-growth window forward while leaving the credit episode fixed.

We keep each GDP-growth window three years long so that we can compare growth over equally long periods. The horizon $h$ tells us how many years we move the window forward. For each horizon, we calculate GDP growth as follows:

$$\mathrm{GDPGrowth}^{(h)}_{i,t}=\mathrm{log\_real\_gdp}_{i,t+h}-\mathrm{log\_real\_gdp}_{i,t+h-3},\qquad h=0,\ldots,5.$$

In the variable names `gdp_3yr_h0` through `gdp_3yr_h5`, `3yr` tells us that each window covers three years, and `h` tells us how many years the window is moved forward. Before looking at the figure below, use the formula to work out which years one later horizon covers.


Quiz: The credit expansion is fixed from t - 3 to t. Which periods does the model with gdp_3yr_h4 compare?

- GDP growth covers t to t + 4, while credit changes cover t - 3 to t. [ ]

- GDP growth covers t + 1 to t + 4, while credit changes cover t - 3 to t. [x]

- GDP growth covers t + 1 to t + 4, while credit changes cover t + 1 to t + 4. [ ]

- GDP growth covers t + 3 to t + 4, while credit changes cover t - 3 to t. [ ]


The figure below compares the GDP-growth windows for all six horizons with the fixed credit window. Each window covers three years. As `h` increases, the GDP-growth window moves forward, while the credit window remains unchanged.
